summaries.example: Imagine making a collection by a rule: “put in every book on this shelf.” NF allows many such collections, but the rule must pass a safety check called stratification. A rule such as “put in every collection that does not contain itself” fails the check because it turns back on itself. The safety check is meant to avoid troublesome paradoxes while still allowing a collection containing everything.
summaries.summary: Quine’s New Foundations is a different way to build set theory. A set is treated as a collection, and two sets are the same if they have the same members. NF also lets us form a set from objects that fit a description, but only when the description passes a safety test called stratification. This test is connected to older type theories, where objects are placed into separate levels. NF removes the separate labels and keeps only descriptions that could have received consistent labels. This makes room for a universal set—the set of everything—without simply allowing every possible description. The entry compares NF with ZF, a more familiar set theory organized around wellfoundedness, meaning that membership does not continue downward forever. NF has unusual results: some ordinary proofs, including the general form of Cantor’s theorem, do not go through in the expected way, and the axiom of choice is rejected. Mathematicians have also studied NFU, a related system that allows urelements, or objects that are not sets. Recent work discussed in the entry reports a consistency proof for NF, although many questions about its mathematics and future importance remain open.
key_ideas: Quine’s New Foundations, usually called NF, is a system of rules for talking about sets.
NF combines a rule about having the same members with a restricted rule for making new sets.
The restriction is called stratification. It acts like assigning safe levels to objects in a description.
NF can have a universal set, while ZF focuses on wellfounded sets and does not have one.
Some familiar mathematics can be represented in NF, but the representation may work differently from the usual ZF version.
summaries.why_it_matters: Set theory is used as a foundation for much of mathematics. NF matters because it asks whether we can avoid dangerous self-reference by controlling the descriptions used to make sets, rather than by allowing only wellfounded sets. It shows that changing the basic rules can preserve some mathematics while changing other results. Studying NF also teaches an important lesson: different logical foundations may describe familiar ideas in different ways.

important_terms.definition: A collection of objects. In set theory, the objects inside a set are called its members.
The idea that two sets are the same when they have exactly the same members.
A safety rule for descriptions of sets. It assigns levels, or types, so membership statements do not loop back in a dangerous way.
The rule that a set may be made from all objects satisfying a safe description.
A set that contains every object in the theory. NF allows this kind of set, unlike standard ZF set theory.
A theory of sets that tries to describe sets whose membership does not go down forever in a chain.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a rule that talks about an object containing itself cause trouble?
Would a universal set be useful? What problems might it create?
Why could assigning levels make a description safer?
Should two collections count as the same whenever they have the same members?

summaries.example: Consider the attempted diagonal proof that no function from X onto the power set of X can exist. In ordinary set theory, one forms D = {x in X: x is not in f(x)}. In NF, the description may fail stratification: the condition that x belongs to X gives x one level, while the condition that f(x) is a subset of X requires related variables to receive incompatible levels. So the usual proof cannot be carried out for arbitrary X. A modified construction using singleton sets can restore a diagonal argument in a related case.
summaries.summary: Quine’s New Foundations (NF) is a one-sorted axiomatic set theory built from two principles. Extensionality identifies sets by their members. Restricted comprehension says that a collection defined by a formula exists when the formula is stratified: one can assign numerical levels to variables so that membership moves up one level and equality preserves level. This restriction comes from type theory, where variables explicitly belong to disjoint levels. NF removes the visible type labels and treats formulas that can be consistently typed as genuine formulas. The related idea of typical ambiguity explains why shifting every type upward should preserve a theorem, but the passage from typed formulas to a one-sorted theory is mathematically nontrivial. NF differs sharply from ZF. ZF is commonly understood as axiomatizing wellfounded sets, with no endlessly descending membership chains. NF instead permits a universal set and other large collections, while some familiar constructions become unavailable because their defining formulas are unstratified. For example, the standard diagonal proof of Cantor’s theorem fails for arbitrary X, although a related diagonal argument works for the set of singletons of elements of X. This leads to the T operation on cardinals and to the notions of cantorian and strongly cantorian sets. The entry also examines NF’s history, its relation to the axiom of choice, fragments and proof theory, implementations of mathematical objects, and NFU. It reports recent work presenting a consistency proof for NF, while emphasizing that the significance and future direction of the theory remain unsettled.
key_ideas: NF has extensionality plus restricted comprehension, with stratification controlling which descriptions define sets.
Its background is type theory: membership connects adjacent levels, and equality connects variables at the same level.
ZF and NF respond to set-theoretic paradoxes differently. ZF emphasizes wellfounded membership; NF emphasizes noncircular descriptions.
Because stratification blocks some definitions, standard results can change. The unrestricted Cantor theorem is not provable in NF by its usual diagonal argument.

NF studies use the T operation to express how singleton formation changes cardinalities. A set is cantorian when its size agrees with the size of its singleton image; strong cantorian behavior requires the restricted singleton function itself to exist.
The entry discusses consistency results, NFU, fragments of NF, proof theory, and ways to interpret mathematics through large or global equivalence-class constructions.
summaries.why_it_matters: NF tests whether set theory can be founded on a syntactic form of noncircularity rather than primarily on wellfoundedness. Its unusual theorems and failed proofs show that foundational choices affect what counts as an available mathematical object and which arguments can be formalized. At the same time, the entry describes ways NF can represent substantial mathematics, sometimes through large sets or global equivalence classes rather than familiar ZF constructions. Comparing NF, ZF, and NFU therefore illuminates the connections among logic, paradox avoidance, mathematical practice, and consistency.

important_terms.definition: The principle that sets with exactly the same members are identical.
A restriction on comprehension requiring variables to receive compatible levels: membership raises a level, while equality keeps levels equal.
The principle that a set exists for every object satisfying an allowed formula; NF permits only stratified instances.
A set theory whose axioms are aimed at sets with no infinite descending membership chains.
The typed theory from which NF is constructed by removing explicit type subscripts while retaining formulas that can be typed consistently.
The principle that a formula and the formula obtained by raising every type one level have the same status.
The operation sending the size of X to the size of the set of singletons of members of X; its behavior is central in NF.
A related theory that weakens extensionality by allowing urelements, objects that are not sets.

What does the failure of the ordinary Cantor proof reveal about the role of comprehension?
Why might a theory treat a universal set as legitimate while making some familiar functions unavailable as sets?
Does a consistency proof settle whether NF is the best foundation for mathematics?
How might strong typing in ordinary mathematics fit with NF’s stratification requirement?

summaries.example: Suppose a class wants to make a collection using the rule “include every student who belongs to their own collection.” The rule is circular: it asks about the collection while trying to create it. NF uses a level-checking idea. If a statement says that one thing belongs to another, the two things must be assigned different levels; if it says they are equal, they must have the same level. A statement such as “x belongs to x” cannot pass this check, but “x belongs to y” can. Thus NF allows many collection-building rules while blocking some risky ones.
summaries.summary: Quine’s New Foundations, or NF, is an alternative foundation for set theory. It begins with extensionality: two sets are identical when they have the same members. It also uses a form of comprehension, the idea that a rule can define a set, but only when the rule is stratified. Stratification means that variables can be assigned levels so that membership links different levels in the right direction, while equality links equal levels. For instance, “x belongs to x” fails the test, whereas “x belongs to y” can pass. This idea comes from type theory, which places objects in separate levels to reduce circularity. NF removes the visible level labels and keeps the descriptions that could be assigned levels consistently. NF differs from ZF, the set theory most often associated with wellfoundedness. In ZF, sets are studied through membership structures that do not descend forever. NF instead allows a universal set, meaning a set of everything, and it can describe some collections that ZF treats only as classes or does not form as sets. These choices have consequences. The ordinary proof of Cantor’s theorem cannot be completed in full generality in NF because the required diagonal collection may not be stratified. NF also refutes the full axiom of choice, while some weaker choice principles remain unresolved in the entry’s discussion. The theory has been examined through typed systems, consistency reductions, model constructions, proof theory, and different implementations of numbers, ordinals, and other mathematical objects. A related theory, NFU, allows urelements—objects that are not sets—and has different results. The entry describes recent work claiming a consistency proof for NF and leaves open how influential the system will become.
key_ideas: NF is Quine’s alternative system of axiomatic set theory, introduced in the 1930s.
It keeps extensionality but restricts comprehension to stratified descriptions.
Stratification grew out of type theory, but NF removes explicit type labels and uses one general universe of sets.
ZF and NF handle the danger of paradox differently: ZF emphasizes wellfounded membership, while NF emphasizes safe descriptions.
NF permits a universal set and has surprising consequences for familiar results such as Cantor’s theorem and the axiom of choice.
Researchers also study NFU, fragments of NF, and ways to represent ordinary mathematics inside these systems.
summaries.why_it_matters: NF matters because it offers a different answer to a central question in the foundations of mathematics: how can we form sets without producing paradoxes? Its answer focuses on the form of descriptions and their hidden level structure. Comparing NF with ZF shows that foundational rules do not merely provide a neutral language; they affect which objects exist and which proofs work. NF also broadens philosophical discussion about whether wellfounded sets are the only legitimate sets and whether a universal set can be mathematically coherent.

important_terms.definition: A collection of things, treated in set theory as objects with members.
The rule that sets with precisely the same members are equal.
A condition for deciding whether a description is safe enough to define a set by assigning compatible levels to its variables.
A principle saying that a collection exists for objects satisfying an acceptable description.
The set containing every object in the theory. NF permits it, whereas ZF does not.
The absence of an endless descending chain of membership, such as x belongs to y, y belongs to z, and so on downward.
A theory that separates objects into levels and permits membership only between neighboring levels.

What advantages could a universal set have? What new questions could it raise?
Why does removing type labels from type theory change the situation?
If a familiar proof fails in NF, does that show the proof was wrong, or that the rules are different?
